Initiative: Reduce the volume and impact of packaging materials used.
Old Initiative: Optimise packaging materials - Reduce packaging materials used, and waste generated
Description: Reduce unnecessary primary, secondary and tertiary packaging while maintaining product protection, food safety and quality. Prioritise eliminating packaging first, followed by reducing material use and selecting lower-impact packaging where packaging remains necessary.
Why/Benefit: Reducing packaging at source lowers material consumption and waste generation and can reduce procurement, transport, storage and waste-management costs. It can also reduce packaging-related Scope 3 emissions and, for obligated UK producers, packaging EPR disposal fees.
How to achieve this: Establish a baseline of packaging used by material and weight. Review primary, secondary and tertiary packaging to identify unnecessary components and opportunities to reduce weight, dimensions or material use without compromising food safety or product quality. Work with suppliers to trial lighter or simplified formats and prioritise reusable, recyclable or recycled-content alternatives where packaging cannot be eliminated. Track packaging use against the baseline and review specifications regularly.
KPI (Measurable Objective): Packaging intensity: kg packaging per unit/product/£ revenue. Packaging reduction: tonnes and % reduction in packaging against baseline. Packaging eliminated: number of packaging components/items removed. Financial: £ packaging procurement/EPR cost avoided annually. Carbon: tCO₂e avoided from packaging reductions.
Evidence/Case Study: Packaging Reduction Programme – Nestlé Nestlé reduced the weight of its total product packaging by 200,000 tonnes in 2022 and removed 14 billion packaging pieces, contributing to an estimated 280,000-tonne reduction in greenhouse gas emissions from packaging changes.
Cost Saving/Cost:
Potential cost saving depends on the packaging material and the organisation’s EPR obligations. For liable producers, reducing in-scope packaging can reduce UK Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) disposal fees. Confirmed 2025–26 base fees are £192/t for glass, £196/t for paper/card, £259/t for steel, £266/t for aluminium, £280/t for wood, £423/t for plastic and £461/t for fibre-based composite packaging. Additional savings may arise from reduced packaging purchasing, transport and waste-management costs, but these should be calculated using organisation-specific data.

Reference: https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/extended-producer-responsibility-for-packaging-2025-base-fees/extended-producer-responsibility-for-packaging-2025-base-fees
Carbon Abatement Potential: Potentially significant and measurable in tCO₂e avoided. As a real-world benchmark, Nestlé reported that reducing total packaging weight by 200,000 tonnes, alongside packaging redesign, contributed to a 280,000 tCO₂e reduction in 2022. For individual businesses, carbon abatement should be calculated using the quantity and material of packaging avoided and an appropriate lifecycle/embodied-carbon factor rather than applying the Nestlé ratio universally.
Time to implement/ROI: Potentially short payback where packaging can simply be eliminated or lightweighted, because savings can arise immediately through lower material purchasing and, where applicable, EPR costs. WRAP reports that UK Plastics Pact members phased out 36,000 tonnes of hard-to-recycle packaging, resulting in £6.2 million in savings from UK packaging Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) fees. Reference: https://www.wrap.ngo/sites/default/files/2025-11/UK-Plastics-Pact-Annual-Report-24-25.pdf
Efficiency/Impact measure: Monitor tonnes of virgin material avoided, % reduction in packaging weight, packaging units/components eliminated, % of packaging reusable or recyclable, and % recycled content. As an external benchmark, WRAP reports that the UK Plastics Pact achieved a 20% reduction in greenhouse gas emissions from virgin plastic since 2018, while average recycled content across plastic packaging reached 28%. Reference: https://www.wrap.ngo/resources/report/uk-plastics-pact-progress-report-202425#download-file

Initiative: Collaborate with suppliers to reduce packaging impacts across the supply chain
Old Initiative: Engage and work with current suppliers to reduce the impact of packaging
Description: Work collaboratively with suppliers to reduce the environmental impact of packaging associated with purchased goods, deliveries and customer-facing products, including through packaging elimination, reduction, reuse, recycled content and improved recyclability.
Why/Benefit: A significant proportion of packaging is determined upstream by suppliers rather than by hospitality businesses themselves. Supplier engagement can therefore identify packaging reductions that businesses cannot achieve independently, reducing packaging waste, associated Scope 3 emissions and potentially procurement, logistics, waste-management and EPR-related costs.
How to achieve this: Identify suppliers responsible for the largest volumes of packaging and engage them to review packaging specifications. Agree opportunities to eliminate unnecessary packaging, reduce material use, increase recycled content and introduce reusable or returnable packaging. Incorporate packaging requirements into procurement specifications and supplier reviews, and track agreed reductions over time.
KPI (Measurable Objective): Supplier engagement: % of priority suppliers engaged on packaging reduction. Packaging reduction: tonnes and % packaging avoided through supplier initiatives. Reuse: % or number of deliveries using reusable/returnable packaging. Financial: £ annual savings generated through supplier packaging improvements. Carbon: tCO₂e avoided through implemented supplier packaging changes.
Evidence/Case Study: Supplier Packaging Collaboration – Tesco                                                      Tesco engaged 1,500 suppliers through its 4Rs approach to remove unnecessary packaging and difficult-to-recycle materials, resulting in one billion pieces of plastic being removed, a 3,480-tonne reduction in its annual packaging footprint, and more than 11,000 tonnes of difficult-to-recycle materials being eliminated.
Cost Saving/Cost: Potentially medium–high, depending on the packaging changes identified. A WRAP hospitality case study at the Millennium Stadium identified potential savings of more than £21,000 per year by working with suppliers to eliminate waste from its supply chain, alongside more than 78 tonnes of waste reduction. This equates to approximately £269 saved per tonne of waste avoided, although the programme covered food and associated packaging waste and should therefore be treated as an indicative benchmark rather than a packaging-only saving. Reference: https://www.wrap.ngo/resources/case-study/tackling-waste-millennium-stadium-case-study
Carbon Abatement Potential: Potentially significant but dependent on the packaging intervention implemented. Supplier collaboration is an enabler; carbon reductions arise from the resulting packaging reduction, reuse, recycled content or redesign. As an industry benchmark, WRAP reported that a 10% reduction in plastic packaging by UK Plastics Pact members between 2018 and 2020 was associated with a reduction of approximately 335,000 tCO₂e. Carbon savings for an individual business should be calculated from the actual packaging change implemented rather than applying this industry-level figure directly. Reference: https://www.wrap.ngo/media-centre/press-releases/uk-plastics-pact-cuts-plastic-packaging-10-and-doubles-recycled-content
Time to implement/ROI: Timing: typically medium term, as changes may require supplier engagement, trials, specification changes and contract/procurement cycles. Some simple packaging-removal measures may deliver savings more quickly. The Millennium Stadium/WRAP programme demonstrates that supplier collaboration can identify recurring annual cost savings, but payback will depend on whether implementation requires new packaging, equipment or logistics arrangements. Reference: https://www.wrap.ngo/resources/case-study/tackling-waste-millennium-stadium-case-study
Efficiency/Impact measure: Track tonnes of packaging avoided, number/% of suppliers implementing packaging improvements, % reusable/returnable packaging, and tonnes of difficult-to-recycle material eliminated. Tesco provides a useful benchmark: its supplier-focused packaging programme removed more than 11,000 tonnes of difficult-to-recycle materials during the period reported. Reference: https://www.tescoplc.com/tesco-removes-one-billion-pieces-of-plastic/

Initiative: Use dispense or refill systems for drinks rather than single-use packaging
Old Initiative: Use dispense options for drinks where possible
Sub-Sector included: All – particularly relevant for hotels, pubs, bars, restaurants, contract caterers and event venues
Description: Replace individually packaged drinks with dispense, tap, keg or refill systems where feasible to reduce reliance on single-use bottles and cans.
Why/Benefit: Dispense and refill systems can reduce single-use packaging, associated carbon emissions and waste, while also reducing beverage purchasing, transport, storage and waste-management costs. High-volume hospitality operations may achieve particularly strong financial and environmental benefits.
How to achieve this: Identify high-volume beverages currently purchased in single-use bottles or cans, such as water, soft drinks, beer and wine. Assess suitable alternatives including filtered water systems, post-mix soft drinks, draught beer and wine-on-tap or keg systems. Compare equipment, maintenance and operating costs against current purchasing and waste costs, trial suitable systems and monitor packaging, cost and carbon savings.
KPI (Measurable Objective): Single-use packaging avoided: number of bottles/cans avoided per year. Packaging reduction: kg/tonnes of packaging avoided. Financial: £ saving per drink and £ annual saving. Carbon: kg/tCO₂e avoided annually. Adoption: % of applicable drinks served through dispense/refill systems.
Evidence/Case Study: Refillable Wine System – Top Cuvée                                                                       Top Cuvée introduced a refillable wine system using kegged wine and reusable bottles at its London venues, generating approximately £29,000 in refillable wine sales over six months while avoiding more than 1,000 single-use wine bottles.
Cost Saving/Cost: £0.27–£1.61 saving per 750ml bottle replaced, depending on the single-use alternative and volume. EcoPure Waters reports that at 200 bottles/day its on-site refill system costs approximately £0.19 per bottle, with savings ranging from £0.27 versus low-cost plastic to £1.61 versus premium glass. At 50 bottles/day, estimated annual savings range from approximately £3,282 to £27,727, depending on the single-use comparator. Reference: https://ecopurewaters.com/insights-the-ecopure-effect-2026/
Carbon Abatement Potential: Approximately 0.31–2.47 tCO₂e/year avoided versus single-use plastic, or 2.92–23.37 tCO₂e/year versus single-use glass, for sites dispensing approximately 25–200 bottles per day according to EcoPure Waters' comparison. For example, at 100 bottles/day, the reported saving is approximately 1.24 tCO₂e/year versus plastic and 11.68 tCO₂e/year versus glass. Actual savings depend on volume and the system being replaced. Reference: https://ecopurewaters.com/insights-the-ecopure-effect-2026/?utm_source=chatgpt.com
Time to implement/ROI: Typical payback: under 12 months, and often under 6 months at higher volumes. EcoPure Waters reports that payback on its system, including branded bottles and ancillary equipment, is generally below 12 months compared with most single-use bottled-water options once usage exceeds approximately 25 bottles/day. At higher volumes, payback can be substantially shorter. Reference: https://ecopurewaters.com/insights-the-ecopure-effect-2026/?utm_source=chatgpt.com
Efficiency/Impact measure: Track single-use bottles avoided per year and packaging avoided per drink served. EcoPure reports that a site dispensing 100 bottles/day could avoid approximately 36,500 single-use bottles annually, increasing to approximately 73,000 bottles annually at 200 bottles/day. Reference: https://ecopurewaters.com/insights-the-ecopure-effect-2026/

Initiative: Undertake life cycle assessment (LCA) of packaging to understand its full environmental impact
Description: Assess the environmental impacts of packaging across its life cycle, including raw material extraction, manufacturing, transport and end-of-life, to identify packaging options with lower overall environmental impacts and avoid shifting impacts between life-cycle stages.
Why/Benefit: Packaging that appears more sustainable based on a single characteristic, such as weight or recyclability, may have greater impacts elsewhere in its life cycle. LCA enables businesses to compare packaging alternatives systematically and identify options that reduce overall environmental impacts while maintaining product protection, food safety and operational performance.
How to achieve this: Prioritise high-volume or high-impact packaging formats for assessment. Define the scope and functional unit, collect data on packaging materials, manufacturing, transport and end-of-life, and compare alternative packaging options using recognised LCA methodology, software or specialist support. Use the findings alongside cost, food-safety and operational considerations when making packaging decisions.
KPI (Measurable Objective): Coverage: % of priority packaging formats assessed using LCA. Improvement: % reduction in lifecycle GHG emissions between existing and proposed packaging. Materials: kg of material avoided per packaging unit. Implementation: % of LCA recommendations implemented. Financial: % reduction in packaging costs following LCA-informed redesign.
Evidence/Case Study: LCA-Informed Packaging Redesign – Household Appliance                                                                                                                                                                                                                             Researchers used Life Cycle Assessment to identify environmental hotspots and redesign packaging for a household appliance, resulting in an average reduction of approximately 30% across the assessed environmental impact categories, including a 68% reduction in land use and a 37% reduction in terrestrial ecotoxicity.
Cost Saving/Cost: LCA itself is an enabling activity; financial savings depend on the packaging changes subsequently implemented. In a Nefab case study, packaging optimisation reduced total packaging costs by 10% compared with the previous design, through material optimisation and reduced weight. Businesses should compare the cost per packaging unit before and after implementing LCA-informed changes. Reference: https://www.nefab.com/news-insights/2025/optimized-packaging-for-motherboards/?utm_source=chatgpt.com
Carbon Abatement Potential: LCA itself does not directly abate carbon; the resulting packaging redesign can. In the Nefab case study, the redesigned packaging achieved a 27% reduction in CO₂ emissions compared with the previous packaging solution, using lighter and recyclable materials. For individual businesses, measure kgCO₂e per packaging unit before vs. after redesign and multiply the difference by annual packaging volumes to estimate total tCO₂e savings. Reference: https://www.nefab.com/news-insights/2025/optimized-packaging-for-motherboards/?utm_source=chatgpt.com
Time to implement/ROI: Project-specific. LCA requires an upfront investment of staff time, data collection, software or external specialist support, so payback depends on the cost of the assessment and savings generated by subsequent packaging changes. The Nefab case demonstrates that LCA-informed/quantified packaging optimisation can generate recurring benefits through a 10% reduction in packaging costs, but the source does not provide implementation cost or payback period; therefore, a specific ROI should not be claimed. Reference: https://www.nefab.com/news-insights/2025/optimized-packaging-for-motherboards/?utm_source=chatgpt.com
Efficiency/Impact measure: Measure environmental impacts beyond carbon where relevant, including material use, land use, ecotoxicity, resource depletion and end-of-life recyclability. In the household-appliance case study, redesigned packaging reduced assessed environmental impacts by approximately 30% on average, including land use by 68% and terrestrial ecotoxicity by 37%. Reference:https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/19397038.2021.1920644?utm_source=chatgpt.com

Initiative: Eliminate single-use plastic items from operations
Sub-Sector included: All – guest amenities particularly relevant for hotels and other accommodation providers
Description: Eliminate avoidable single-use plastic items and packaging from operations and replace them with reusable or refillable alternatives where practical, while maintaining food safety, hygiene, product quality and customer experience.
Why/Benefit: Eliminating single-use plastics reduces material consumption, packaging waste and associated lifecycle emissions. Reusable and refillable alternatives can also reduce recurring purchasing and waste-management costs. In England, certain single-use plastic items are already banned or restricted, including plastic cutlery, drink stirrers and expanded/extruded polystyrene food and drink containers.
How to achieve this: Audit single-use plastic items across operations and quantify annual usage by item and weight. Prioritise items that can be eliminated completely, followed by those that can be replaced with reusable or refillable systems. For example, replace hotel toiletry miniatures with bulk dispensers, bottled water with refill systems, and disposable serviceware with reusable alternatives. Update procurement specifications, engage suppliers and track reductions against the baseline.
KPI (Measurable Objective): Plastic eliminated: kg/tonnes of single-use plastic avoided annually. Items eliminated: number of single-use plastic items avoided annually. Reduction: % reduction in single-use plastic against baseline. Financial: £ annual purchasing/waste costs avoided. Carbon: tCO₂e avoided through elimination/reuse.
Evidence/Case Study: Elimination of Bathroom Miniatures – IHG Hotels & Resorts                                                                                                         IHG committed to replacing bathroom miniatures with bulk-size amenities across more than 5,600 hotels and nearly 843,000 guest rooms, which was expected to eliminate approximately 200 million bathroom miniatures from use each year.
Cost Saving/Cost: Potentially significant where single-use products are replaced by refill systems. Boston Harbor Hotel replaced purchased bottled water with an on-site bottling system, reducing annual programme costs from $10,901 to $4,420 – a saving of $6,481 per year, or 60% – while avoiding more than 10,000 disposable bottles annually. Savings for other single-use items will depend on the replacement system and usage volumes. Reference: https://vivreauwater.com/water-dispensers/blog/case-study/the-boston-harbor-hotel/?utm_source=chatgpt.com
Carbon Abatement Potential: Potentially significant but dependent on the item and replacement system. ReLondon modelling found that reducing single-use packaging through elimination and reuse could reduce lifecycle emissions substantially: 80% elimination of fruit and vegetable packaging corresponded to an 80% emissions reduction, while reuse of food packaging in restaurants was modelled at a 32% emissions reduction. Reusable takeaway packaging scenarios produced reductions ranging from 13% to 75%, depending on packaging category. Businesses should calculate the net carbon impact of the specific single-use item and its replacement rather than applying one generic factor. Reference: https://relondon.gov.uk/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/Londons-packaging-footprint-report.pdf
Time to implement/ROI: Potentially short where high-volume single-use purchases are replaced with reusable/refillable systems. The Boston Harbor Hotel example achieved recurring annual savings of $6,481 (60%) after replacing purchased bottled water with an on-site system. The source demonstrates financial savings but does not provide the initial equipment cost, so a specific payback period should not be claimed. Businesses should calculate ROI as implementation cost ÷ annual purchasing and waste-management savings. Reference: https://vivreauwater.com/water-dispensers/blog/case-study/the-boston-harbor-hotel/?utm_source=chatgpt.com
Efficiency/Impact measure: Track number of single-use items avoided, kg/tonnes of material avoided, and % of applicable items converted to reusable/refillable formats. IHG's programme provides a useful scale benchmark of approximately 200 million bathroom miniatures avoided annually once implemented across its estate. Reference: https://www.ihgplc.com/en/news-and-media/news-releases/2019/end-of-the-road-for-bathroom-miniatures-as-ihg-opts-for-bulk-size--amenities-to-reduce-plastic-waste?utm_source=chatgpt.com

Initiative: Increase recycled content in packaging materials
Sub-Sector included: All – particularly relevant for breweries, pubs/bars and businesses using high volumes of packaged products
Description: Increase the proportion of recycled material used in packaging, including plastic, glass, aluminium, paper and cardboard, where food safety, quality and performance requirements allow.
Why/Benefit: Increasing recycled content reduces demand for virgin raw materials and can lower the lifecycle carbon footprint of packaging. For plastic packaging, it can also provide a financial benefit through the UK Plastic Packaging Tax where applicable.
How to achieve this: Establish the current recycled content of key packaging formats and identify high-volume packaging with low or no recycled content. Work with packaging suppliers to increase recycled content while maintaining food safety, quality and performance. Prioritise high-volume materials and incorporate minimum recycled-content requirements into procurement specifications and supplier reviews.
KPI (Measurable Objective): Recycled content: % recycled content by packaging material. Virgin material avoided: tonnes/year. Coverage: % of packaging meeting minimum recycled-content requirements. Financial: £ Plastic Packaging Tax avoided where applicable. Carbon: tCO₂e avoided through substitution of virgin material.
Evidence/Case Study: Recycled Content in Bread Bags – Kingsmill                                                            Kingsmill introduced 30% post-consumer recycled content into selected bread bags through the UK Plastics Pact, removing the equivalent of more than two million virgin plastic bags from its supply chain since August 2021.
Cost Saving/Cost: Potential saving: £228.82 per tonne of qualifying plastic packaging. From 1 April 2026, UK Plastic Packaging Tax is charged at £228.82/t on finished plastic packaging components containing less than 30% recycled plastic, where the relevant manufacturer/importer is liable. Packaging containing at least 30% recycled plastic is not chargeable. Therefore, moving 10 tonnes of qualifying plastic packaging from below 30% to at least 30% recycled content could avoid £2,288.20 in PPT, before considering any difference in material price. Reference: https://www.gov.uk/guidance/check-if-you-need-to-register-for-plastic-packaging-tax?utm_source=chatgpt.com
Carbon Abatement Potential: Approximately 2.2–3.7% lower lifecycle GHG emissions for every 10 percentage-point increase in recycled content in plastic packaging, depending on the polymer. Therefore, increasing recycled content from 0% to 30% could reduce packaging lifecycle emissions by approximately 6.6–11.1%. Actual savings should be calculated for the specific polymer and packaging format. Reference: https://relondon.gov.uk/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/Londons-packaging-footprint-report.pdf?utm_source=chatgpt.com
Time to implement/ROI: Potentially immediate for businesses directly liable for Plastic Packaging Tax where qualifying packaging moves from below 30% to at least 30% recycled plastic, subject to any difference in packaging procurement cost. ROI should compare any additional cost of recycled-content packaging against £228.82/t of PPT avoided plus other operational benefits. Where the hospitality business is not itself the manufacturer or importer liable for PPT, financial benefits may instead be reflected indirectly through supplier pricing. Reference: https://www.gov.uk/green-taxes-and-reliefs/plastic-packaging-tax?utm_source=chatgpt.com
Efficiency/Impact measure: Track tonnes of virgin material displaced and average recycled content (%). As a wider industry benchmark, UK Plastics Pact members reached 28% average recycled content across plastic packaging in 2024/25, while PET bottles reached 51%. Reference: https://www.wrap.ngo/resources/report/uk-plastics-pact-progress-report-202425?utm_source=chatgpt.com

Initiative: Evaluate equipment purchases based on full life-cycle cost and environmental impact
Old Initiative: Consider the full lifecycle costs and impacts of equipment at purchase
Sub-Sector included: All – particularly relevant for hotels, contract caterers, restaurants and other equipment-intensive operations
Description: Evaluate equipment based on its total cost and environmental impact over its expected lifetime rather than purchase price alone, considering acquisition, energy and water consumption, maintenance, lifespan and end-of-life costs.
Why/Benefit: Equipment with a higher upfront cost may have a lower total cost of ownership and environmental impact if it uses less energy and water, requires less maintenance or lasts longer. Life-cycle costing helps businesses identify the option offering the best overall financial and environmental performance over its useful life.
How to achieve this: For significant equipment purchases, compare shortlisted options using a standard life-cycle cost assessment. Include purchase and installation costs, expected energy and water consumption, maintenance and repair costs, expected lifespan and end-of-life costs or residual value. Where data are available, compare lifecycle carbon impacts alongside financial costs and incorporate LCC criteria into procurement decisions.
KPI (Measurable Objective): Coverage: % of significant equipment purchases assessed using LCC. Financial: £ lifetime cost and £ lifetime saving versus alternative equipment. Energy: kWh/year and lifetime kWh saved. Water: m³/year saved where relevant. Carbon: tCO₂e avoided over expected equipment life. Performance: expected equipment lifespan and maintenance cost/year.
Evidence/Case Study: Life-Cycle Approach to Catering Equipment – Carbon Trust The Carbon Trust identified that taking a more strategic approach to catering operations, including equipment selection and use, could reduce energy consumption by more than 30%, equivalent to more than £250 million in annual energy-cost savings and more than one million tonnes of carbon annually across the UK catering sector.
Cost Saving/Cost: Potentially significant for energy-intensive equipment. The Carbon Trust estimated that a more strategic approach to catering operations, including equipment selection and use, could reduce energy consumption by more than 30%, saving the UK catering sector over £250 million per year, equivalent to more than 3p per meal served. For individual purchases, compare £ total lifetime cost between equipment options rather than upfront price alone. Reference: https://www.carbontrust.com/news-and-insights/news/uk-catering-industry-missing-out-on-more-than-a-quarter-of-a-billion-pounds-in-energy-savings-every-year-warns-the-carbon-trust?utm_source=chatgpt.com
Carbon Abatement Potential: Potentially significant for energy-intensive equipment. The Carbon Trust estimated that improved catering operations, including more efficient equipment selection and use, could avoid more than one million tonnes of carbon annually across the UK catering sector. At business level, calculate carbon abatement as the difference in lifetime energy consumption between equipment options × applicable energy emissions factor. Reference: https://www.carbontrust.com/news-and-insights/news/uk-catering-industry-missing-out-on-more-than-a-quarter-of-a-billion-pounds-in-energy-savings-every-year-warns-the-carbon-trust?utm_source=chatgpt.com
Time to implement/ROI: Equipment-specific. A higher upfront purchase price can be offset over the equipment's lifetime through lower energy, water, maintenance and replacement costs. Calculate simple payback = additional upfront cost ÷ annual operating-cost saving, and compare total costs over the expected equipment life. The European Commission recommends including purchase, installation, energy/water use, maintenance and end-of-life costs or residual value when evaluating LCC. Reference: https://green-forum.ec.europa.eu/green-business/green-public-procurement/life-cycle-costing_en?utm_source=chatgpt.com
Efficiency/Impact measure: Compare annual energy consumption (kWh), annual water consumption (m³), maintenance costs (£/year), expected lifespan (years) and end-of-life/residual value between equipment options. The European Commission identifies energy, water/fuel, maintenance/replacement and disposal as key areas where life-cycle costing can identify savings. Reference: https://green-forum.ec.europa.eu/green-business/green-public-procurement/life-cycle-costing_en?utm_source=chatgpt.com

Initiative: Shift from equipment ownership to service or leasing models
Old Initiative: Switch from ownership to service leasing model
Sub-Sector included: All – particularly relevant for equipment-intensive operations such as hotels, contract caterers and breweries
Description: Use service or leasing models instead of purchasing equipment outright where appropriate, with providers retaining responsibility for maintenance, performance, upgrades and end-of-life recovery or reuse.
Why/Benefit: Service and leasing models can reduce upfront capital requirements and transfer responsibility for equipment maintenance and end-of-life management to the provider. Where contracts incentivise durability, repair and reuse, they can also extend equipment life, reduce material consumption and support more circular asset management.
How to achieve this: Identify equipment suitable for service or leasing models, such as lighting, coffee machines, laundry equipment, refrigeration and HVAC. Compare the whole-life cost and environmental impact of leasing/service contracts against outright purchase. Prioritise providers offering maintenance, repair, performance guarantees, upgrades and end-of-life take-back, reuse or recycling, and include these requirements in procurement contracts.
KPI (Measurable Objective): Adoption: % of suitable equipment under service/leasing models. Financial: £ upfront capital avoided and £ annual/lifetime cost versus ownership. Energy: kWh/year saved. Carbon: tCO₂e avoided. Circularity: % of equipment/materials returned for reuse, refurbishment or recycling at end of contract.
Evidence/Case Study: Light as a Service – Schiphol Airport Schiphol Airport adopted a Light as a Service model for Lounge 2, paying for the light used while Philips retained ownership of 3,700 lighting fixtures and responsibility for their performance, durability and end-of-life reuse or recycling. The new LED system reduced electricity consumption by 50% compared with conventional lighting, while the redesigned fixtures were expected to last 75% longer.
Cost Saving/Cost: Potential benefit: avoided upfront capital expenditure plus energy and maintenance savings. Under Light as a Service, businesses pay a service fee rather than making a major upfront investment in the lighting system. Signify states that its model can provide no upfront investment and generate immediate energy and maintenance savings. Actual £ savings depend on the contract, existing equipment and energy consumption, so a universal £ saving should not be claimed. Reference: https://www.signify.com/en-gb/signify-services/managed-services/light-as-a-service?utm_source=chatgpt.com
Carbon Abatement Potential: Equipment-specific; the service model enables rather than directly causes the carbon reduction. At Schiphol, the LED system installed through Light as a Service reduced electricity consumption by 50% compared with conventional lighting, reducing associated operational emissions. Businesses should calculate tCO₂e avoided from the difference in annual energy consumption between the previous and service-based equipment × applicable emissions factor. Reference: https://www.signify.com/en-in/our-company/news/press-release-archive/2015/20150416-Philips-provides-Light-as-a-Service-to-Schiphol-Airport?utm_source=chatgpt.com
Time to implement/ROI: Potential financial benefit from the start of the contract where the model avoids upfront investment and delivers immediate operating savings. Signify states that its Light as a Service model requires no upfront investment and can generate positive cash flow through energy and maintenance savings. Actual ROI and contract length are equipment- and provider-specific and should be compared against the whole-life cost of ownership. Reference: https://www.signify.com/en-gb/signify-services/managed-services/light-as-a-service?utm_source=chatgpt.com
Efficiency/Impact measure: Measure equipment lifespan, maintenance requirements and end-of-life recovery/reuse alongside energy performance. At Schiphol, the redesigned lighting fixtures were expected to last 75% longer than conventional fixtures, while Signify retained responsibility for their reuse or recycling at end of life. Reference: https://www.signify.com/en-in/our-company/news/press-release-archive/2015/20150416-Philips-provides-Light-as-a-Service-to-Schiphol-Airport?utm_source=chatgpt.com

Initiative: Prioritise reused, refurbished and responsibly sourced furniture and fittings
Sub-Sector included: All – particularly relevant for hotels, restaurants, pubs/bars and other businesses undertaking refurbishments or fit-outs
Description: Prioritise the reuse, repair and refurbishment of existing furniture and fittings before purchasing new items. Where new products are required, select durable, repairable products made from recycled or responsibly sourced materials.
Why/Benefit: Reusing and refurbishing furniture extends asset life, avoids waste and reduces the need for new materials and manufacturing, lowering embodied carbon. It can also reduce procurement and disposal costs. Where new furniture is necessary, responsible sourcing can reduce environmental impacts and support more sustainable material supply chains.
How to achieve this: Audit existing furniture and fittings before purchasing new items and identify what can be retained, repaired, refurbished or redistributed. Where additional furniture is required, consider reused or remanufactured products before buying new. For new purchases, prioritise durable and repairable products containing recycled or responsibly sourced materials and request recognised certification where relevant, such as FSC-certified timber. Incorporate reuse, durability, repairability and end-of-life requirements into procurement specifications.
KPI (Measurable Objective): Reuse: % of furniture requirements met through existing/reused/refurbished assets. Waste: number and tonnes of furniture items diverted from disposal. Financial: £ saved versus equivalent new furniture. Carbon: kg/tCO₂e avoided versus purchasing new. Responsible sourcing: % of new furniture meeting specified sustainability/certification requirements.
Evidence/Case Study: Furniture Reuse and Refurbishment – Crown Workspace Crown Workspace refurbished and remanufactured more than 125,000 desks, chairs and other furniture items, diverting more than 2,800 tonnes of furniture into reuse and avoiding more than 7,100 tCO₂e compared with disposal and replacement with new furniture.
Cost Saving/Cost: Potential saving: approximately 70–80% versus equivalent new furniture. Crown Workspace reports that refurbished and remanufactured office furniture typically costs 70–80% less than equivalent new items. Additional savings may arise from avoided disposal and replacement costs. Actual savings will depend on furniture type, condition, refurbishment requirements and transport. Initiative: Extend equipment life and manage WEEE through repair, refurbishment, reuse and responsible recycling
Old Initiative: Adopt a Circular approach for Waste Electrical and Electronic Equipment (WEEE)
Sub-Sector included: All – particularly relevant for equipment-intensive operations such as hotels, contract caterers, breweries and restaurants
Description: Extend the useful life of electrical and electronic equipment through maintenance, repair, refurbishment and redeployment wherever practical. Where equipment can no longer be reused, ensure it is managed through appropriate WEEE recovery and recycling routes.
Why/Benefit: Extending equipment life delays replacement purchases, reduces demand for new equipment and avoids some of the embodied carbon associated with manufacturing new assets. Repair and refurbishment can also reduce procurement costs, while responsible WEEE management keeps reusable components and valuable materials in circulation and supports regulatory compliance.
How to achieve this: Maintain an asset register and identify equipment suitable for maintenance, repair, refurbishment or internal redeployment before replacement. Compare repair/refurbishment costs with replacement costs and remaining useful life. Where equipment is no longer required, assess whether it can be reused or refurbished before treating it as waste. For genuine WEEE, use appropriate authorised collection/treatment routes and maintain records of equipment reused, refurbished and recycled.
KPI (Measurable Objective): Asset life: average equipment lifespan/years extended. Reuse: % of equipment repaired, refurbished or redeployed rather than replaced. Financial: £ avoided replacement expenditure. Carbon: tCO₂e avoided versus purchasing new equipment. WEEE: tonnes/% of end-of-life electrical equipment sent to appropriate reuse/recovery/recycling routes.
Evidence/Case Study: Circular Technology Procurement – Defra Defra reported that refurbished and remanufactured technology devices can cost up to 40% less than new equivalents and deliver an estimated 44% reduction in carbon emissions compared with buying new, demonstrating the financial and carbon benefits of extending equipment life.
Cost Saving/Cost: Up to 40% lower purchase cost for refurbished/remanufactured ICT devices compared with new equivalents. This provides an indicative benchmark for laptops, tablets and mobile devices. Savings for commercial kitchen equipment, refrigeration, HVAC and other electrical assets should be calculated by comparing repair/refurbishment costs with replacement costs and remaining useful life. Reference: https://sustainableict.blog.gov.uk/2026/02/18/how-were-making-technology-procurement-more-sustainable/
Carbon Abatement Potential: Approximately 44% lower carbon emissions for refurbished/remanufactured ICT devices compared with purchasing new, according to Defra's circular technology procurement programme. This should be treated as an ICT-specific benchmark rather than applied to all equipment. For other assets, compare the embodied and operational carbon impacts of repair/refurbishment with replacement. Reference: https://sustainableict.blog.gov.uk/2026/02/18/how-were-making-technology-procurement-more-sustainable/
Time to implement/ROI: Potentially immediate where refurbished equipment is purchased at a lower cost than new equipment. Defra reports savings of up to 40% compared with new ICT devices, meaning a financial benefit can arise at the point of purchase. For repairing existing equipment, ROI should compare repair/refurbishment costs and expected remaining life against the cost of replacement. Reference: https://sustainableict.blog.gov.uk/2026/02/18/how-were-making-technology-procurement-more-sustainable/
Efficiency/Impact measure: Track years of equipment life extended, number/% of assets repaired or refurbished, tonnes of WEEE avoided through reuse and tonnes sent for appropriate recovery/recycling. Environment Agency guidance prioritises reuse of whole appliances, followed by reuse of components where possible, before material recycling. Reference: https://www.gov.uk/guidance/waste-electrical-and-electronic-equipment-weee-reuse-and-treatment

Initiative: Set responsible sourcing standards for packaging procurement
Old Initiative: Opt for sustainably produced products made using eco-conscious methods and reclaimed materials
Description: Establish procurement standards that prioritise packaging made from responsibly sourced, recycled or renewable materials and that is designed for recyclability, while maintaining food safety, product quality and regulatory compliance.
Why/Benefit: Responsible packaging procurement can reduce reliance on virgin materials, improve traceability and support more sustainable material supply chains. Certification can provide evidence that materials such as paper and cardboard originate from responsibly managed or recycled sources, while designing for recyclability can also reduce exposure to higher UK EPR fees.
How to achieve this: Review packaging procurement specifications and establish minimum sustainability requirements by material. Require suppliers to provide evidence of material composition, recycled content and responsible sourcing, using recognised certification such as FSC for relevant paper/cardboard packaging. Include recyclability requirements in specifications and use the UK's Recyclability Assessment Methodology (RAM) where applicable. Review supplier compliance and update requirements as better packaging options become available.
KPI (Measurable Objective): Responsible sourcing: % of applicable packaging with recognised responsible-sourcing certification. Supplier compliance: % of packaging suppliers meeting procurement standards. Recyclability: % of packaging rated Green under RAM where applicable. Materials: % recycled/renewable content. Improvement: tonnes/% of non-compliant or poorly recyclable packaging replaced.
Evidence/Case Study: Responsible Paper and Packaging Sourcing – FSC FSC certification enables businesses to source paper and packaging from responsibly managed forests and/or recycled sources, while chain-of-custody certification provides traceability through the supply chain and evidence to support responsible sourcing requirements.
Cost Saving/Cost: Cost impact is material- and supplier-specific; responsibly sourced materials do not necessarily provide a direct procurement saving. However, recyclability is increasingly linked to EPR costs. From 2026–27, UK EPR disposal fees are modulated according to recyclability, with Red-rated packaging charged more and Green-rated packaging receiving lower fees. For 2026–27, Red-rated packaging is subject to a 1.2× modulation factor relative to the Amber fee, providing a financial incentive to procure more recyclable packaging. Reference: https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/extended-producer-responsibility-for-packaging-modulated-disposal-fees/packuk-extended-producer-responsibility-epr-for-packaging-producer-disposal-fees-modulation-statement?utm_source=chatgpt.com
Carbon Abatement Potential: Packaging-specific; no single carbon-abatement factor should be applied. Carbon savings depend on the material being replaced, recycled/renewable content, packaging weight, manufacturing process and end-of-life route. Businesses should compare kgCO₂e per packaging unit between existing and proposed packaging using supplier-specific lifecycle data or recognised LCA data where available.
Time to implement/ROI: Supplier- and packaging-specific. Updating procurement specifications can be incorporated into normal supplier tendering and contract-review cycles, while implementation timing will depend on availability, testing and existing contracts. For organisations liable for EPR disposal fees, improved recyclability can increasingly provide a financial benefit: modulation begins in 2026–27, with the Red-packaging factor increasing from 1.2× in 2026–27 to 1.6× in 2027–28 and 2.0× in 2028–29. Reference: https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/extended-producer-responsibility-for-packaging-modulated-disposal-fees/packuk-extended-producer-responsibility-epr-for-packaging-producer-disposal-fees-modulation-statement?utm_source=chatgpt.com
Efficiency/Impact measure: Track % of relevant paper/card packaging that is FSC-certified or from recycled sources, alongside supplier compliance and packaging recyclability. FSC certification provides chain-of-custody traceability that helps businesses demonstrate responsible sourcing and implement sustainability procurement policies. Reference: https://uk.fsc.org/packaging?utm_source=chatgpt.com

Initiative: Procure lower-impact staff uniforms and operational textiles
Sub-Sector included: All – particularly relevant for hotels, restaurants, pubs/bars and contract caterers with high volumes of uniforms, linen and towels
Description: Procure uniforms, linen, towels and other operational textiles with lower lifecycle impacts by prioritising durability, responsible or recycled materials, repairability, reuse and appropriate end-of-life recovery.
Why/Benefit: Textiles contribute to Scope 3 emissions through raw material production, manufacturing and end-of-life treatment. Selecting durable, lower-impact textiles and extending their useful life can reduce demand for virgin materials, avoid replacement purchases and reduce textile waste and associated carbon emissions.
How to achieve this: Review procurement specifications for uniforms, linen, towels and other high-volume textiles. Prioritise durable products containing recycled or responsibly sourced fibres and request recognised certification where relevant, such as GOTS, GRS, OEKO-TEX or FSC for applicable fibres/materials. Include durability and repairability criteria in tenders, avoid unnecessary replacement, and establish systems to collect, repair, reuse, redistribute or recycle textiles at end of use.
KPI (Measurable Objective): Sustainable procurement: % of textile purchases meeting defined sustainability standards. Recycled/responsible content: % by weight. Asset life: average lifespan/replacement frequency of uniforms and linen. Reuse: % of textiles repaired/reused/redeployed. Waste: kg/tonnes of textiles diverted from disposal. Carbon: kg/tCO₂e avoided through reuse or lower-impact procurement.
Evidence/Case Study: Lower-Impact Staff Uniforms – Hilton London Metropole Hilton London Metropole introduced staff uniforms made from organic and recycled materials, including recycled polyester produced from post-consumer plastics. The recycled polyester fabric was reported to use more than 50% less energy and around one-third less CO₂ than conventional PET production.
Cost Saving/Cost: Product-specific; no robust universal procurement saving should be assumed. Lower-impact textiles may cost more or less upfront depending on material, supplier and specification. Financial benefits are more likely to arise from greater durability, repair and reuse, which reduce replacement purchases. Businesses should compare £ cost per use or £ cost per year of useful life, rather than purchase price alone. WRAP identifies textile recovery and reuse as offering potential cost savings and economic value, but does not provide a universal £ saving applicable to hospitality uniforms. Reference: https://www.wrap.ngo/resources/case-study/textiles-reports-and-trials?utm_source=chatgpt.com
Carbon Abatement Potential: Material- and intervention-specific. In the Hilton London Metropole example, the recycled polyester used for uniforms was reported to generate around one-third less CO₂ than conventional PET production, alongside more than 50% lower energy use. Reuse can provide additional savings by avoiding manufacture of replacement garments. As a separate workwear benchmark, British Cycling reports approximately 4 kg of embedded carbon per kg of polyester sportswear, illustrating the carbon that can potentially be avoided by keeping suitable garments in use rather than replacing them. References: https://pciaw.org/hilton-london-metropole-hotel-the-sustainable-venue-of-pciaw-summit-awards/?utm_source=chatgpt.com   https://www.britishcycling.org.uk/article/20250205-British-Cycling-and-Stuff4Life-reduce-carbon-emissions-by-rebranding-teamwear-0?utm_source=chatgpt.com
Time to implement/ROI: Product-specific. ROI depends on any difference in purchase price, garment lifespan and avoided replacement costs. For uniforms, assess cost per wear/use over the expected life of the garment, incorporating repair and reuse. Extending garment life can reduce the frequency of replacement purchases, but the available evidence does not support a universal payback period, so I would not claim one.
Efficiency/Impact measure: Track energy/material impacts of selected textiles, garment lifespan, repair/reuse rates and textile waste avoided. In the Hilton example, recycled polyester fabric was reported to use more than 50% less energy than conventional PET production. As a circularity example, a British Cycling/Stuff4Life project rebranded just under 200 kg of existing garments, avoiding approximately 750 kg of end-of-life carbon emissions and generating more than £30,000 in estimated social impact value. References: https://pciaw.org/hilton-london-metropole-hotel-the-sustainable-venue-of-pciaw-summit-awards/?utm_source=chatgpt.com. https://www.circularonline.co.uk/case-studies/building-a-circular-economy-for-workwear/?utm_source=chatgpt.com

Sub-Sector included: All – particularly relevant for hotels, restaurants, pubs/bars, contract caterers and other operations with high cleaning-product use
Description: Procure effective cleaning products with lower environmental impacts by considering chemical formulation, concentration and dosing, packaging, refillability and recognised environmental certification.
Why/Benefit: Environmentally preferable cleaning products can reduce chemical and packaging use, waste and associated environmental impacts. Concentrated and refillable systems can also reduce the volume of product purchased, transported and stored, while accurate dosing can prevent overuse and unnecessary cost.
How to achieve this: Review high-volume cleaning products and identify opportunities to switch to concentrated, refillable or lower-impact alternatives. Prioritise products carrying credible environmental certifications, such as the EU Ecolabel, where appropriate. Introduce controlled dosing or dilution systems for concentrates, work with suppliers to reduce packaging and increase refill/reuse, and train staff to use the correct product and dose while maintaining required hygiene and food-safety standards.
KPI (Measurable Objective): Procurement: % of cleaning spend/products meeting defined environmental criteria. Chemical use: litres/kg of cleaning concentrate used per room, cover or m² cleaned. Packaging: kg/number of cleaning-product containers avoided. Cost: £ cleaning-product cost per room/cover/m². Dosing: % correct dosing/compliance.
Evidence/Case Study: EU Ecolabel Cleaning Products – European Commission EU Ecolabel criteria for cleaning products address environmental impacts including hazardous substances, sustainably sourced raw materials, packaging and fitness for use, providing businesses with a recognised framework for identifying lower-impact cleaning products while maintaining cleaning performance.
Cost Saving/Cost: Product- and system-specific. Concentrated products and controlled dosing can reduce product consumption and packaging, but a universal £ saving should not be assumed. Businesses should compare £ cost per usable/diluted litre and £ cleaning-product cost per room, cover or m² cleaned, rather than purchase price per container. Savings should be calculated from reduced chemical consumption, packaging, deliveries and waste.
Carbon Abatement Potential: Product-specific; no robust universal carbon-abatement factor should be applied. Carbon benefits can arise from reduced chemical production, packaging and transport when concentrated/refillable products replace conventional formats. Businesses should compare kgCO₂e per functional unit of cleaning service using supplier-specific lifecycle data where available, rather than assuming all certified or concentrated products provide the same carbon reduction.
Time to implement/ROI: Potentially short where concentrated products and dosing systems reduce chemical consumption without significant capital investment, but evidence is product-specific. Calculate simple payback as dosing/refill equipment and implementation cost ÷ annual chemical, packaging and delivery savings. Where no equipment is required, savings may begin immediately following the procurement change.
Efficiency/Impact measure: Track chemical consumption per room/cover/m² cleaned, packaging avoided, dilution accuracy and cleaning performance. Environmental improvements should not compromise hygiene or efficacy; EU Ecolabel cleaning-product criteria include fitness-for-use requirements alongside environmental criteria. Reference: https://environment.ec.europa.eu/topics/circular-economy-topics/eu-ecolabel/product-groups-and-criteria/cleaning_en

Initiative: Reduce office paper use and office consumables
Description: Reduce unnecessary paper and office consumable use by prioritising digital processes, controlling printing and procuring recycled or lower-impact products where physical materials remain necessary.
Why/Benefit: Reducing paper and consumable use lowers purchasing and printing costs, reduces waste and decreases the environmental impacts associated with paper production, toner, printing and disposal. Digital workflows can also improve document accessibility and administrative efficiency.
How to achieve this: Replace paper-based processes with digital documentation, e-signatures and electronic workflows where practical. Set printers to double-sided and black-and-white by default, introduce secure/pull printing where appropriate, monitor print volumes and remove unnecessary printers. Where printing remains necessary, procure recycled paper and lower-impact office consumables and track usage against a baseline.
KPI (Measurable Objective): Paper use: sheets or reams per employee/year. Reduction: % reduction in print volume against baseline. Financial: £ annual paper, toner and print-cost savings. Digitalisation: % of applicable processes completed digitally. Waste: kg/tonnes of paper avoided.
Evidence/Case Study: Print Reduction Programme – Leeds City Council Leeds City Council rationalised its printer fleet and introduced more efficient print management, reducing print volume by 25% in the first year, avoiding 12,565,709 A4 sheets of paper and delivering approximately £61,570 in financial savings.
Cost Saving/Cost: £61,570 in paper-related financial savings in the Leeds City Council case study, alongside 12.6 million A4 sheets avoided. The programme also reduced electricity costs by approximately £12,000. Actual savings will depend on paper, toner, print-management and equipment costs. Reference: https://www.gca.gov.uk/news/casestudy-leeds-city-council-becoming-the-best-with-less?utm_source=chatgpt.com
Carbon Abatement Potential: Site-specific. Carbon savings arise from reduced paper production, printing, consumables and waste, but the Leeds case does not provide a quantified tCO₂e figure. Businesses should measure the number/weight of sheets avoided and apply an appropriate paper lifecycle emissions factor where available. I would avoid inventing a generic carbon factor here.
Time to implement/ROI: Potentially short, because behavioural and printer-setting changes can often be implemented with limited capital expenditure. In a UK government example, default double-sided printing contributed to a 37% reduction in paper use at the Department for Transport, while one major paper-using section reduced its paper use by 46% after switching printers to default duplex. Reference: https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/government/uploads/system/uploads/attachment_data/file/69624/pb13846-greening-government-commitments.pdf?utm_source=chatgpt.com
Efficiency/Impact measure: Track print volume per employee, number of printing devices, colour vs black-and-white printing and digital workflow adoption. Leeds City Council reduced its printer fleet by 39% and print volume by 25% in the first year, while Harrow Council cut black-and-white printing by 21% and colour printing by 42%. References:  https://www.gca.gov.uk/news/casestudy-leeds-city-council-becoming-the-best-with-less and https://www.xerox.com/en-rs/services/managed-print/insights/harrow-council-case-study

Initiative: Measure and reduce emissions from purchased goods and services
Old Initiative: Review the impact of emissions associated with the other goods and services that you purchase
Description: Measure greenhouse gas emissions associated with purchased goods and services and use the results to prioritise lower-carbon products, services and suppliers and target the largest Scope 3 emissions sources.
Why/Benefit: Purchased goods and services can represent a significant source of Scope 3 emissions. Measuring these emissions helps businesses identify procurement hotspots, focus supplier engagement on the areas with the greatest potential impact and integrate carbon performance into purchasing decisions.
How to achieve this: Use procurement and spend data to identify major purchased goods and services categories. Estimate emissions initially using recognised spend- or activity-based emission factors, replacing estimates with supplier-specific or product carbon-footprint data where available. Rank categories by emissions, prioritise the largest hotspots, engage key suppliers on emissions data and reduction plans, and incorporate carbon criteria into tenders, supplier selection and contract reviews.
KPI (Measurable Objective): Total emissions: tCO₂e from purchased goods and services/year. Intensity: kgCO₂e per £ spent or appropriate physical unit. Coverage: % of procurement spend covered by emissions measurement. Supplier data: % of priority suppliers providing primary emissions data. Reduction: % change in purchased-goods-and-services emissions against baseline.
Evidence/Case Study: Supply Chain Emissions Programme – Tesco Tesco engages suppliers through its Supplier Network and requires major suppliers to report emissions data and establish climate targets, using supplier engagement to address emissions across its value chain and support progress towards its Scope 3 reduction targets.
Cost Saving/Cost: Enabling initiative – no universal direct cost saving. Measuring procurement emissions can identify opportunities to reduce material, energy and purchasing costs, but savings arise from the subsequent procurement changes rather than emissions measurement itself. Costs may include emissions-data tools, supplier engagement and staff time. Financial impact should therefore be measured as £ savings generated by procurement changes identified through the assessment.
Carbon Abatement Potential: Enabling initiative – carbon reduction depends on actions taken after identifying procurement hotspots. The GHG Protocol recommends assessing purchased goods and services using supplier-specific, hybrid, average-data or spend-based methods. Businesses should establish baseline tCO₂e from purchased goods and services and measure the absolute and percentage reduction resulting from supplier/product changes. Reference: https://ghgprotocol.org/scope-3-calculation-guidance-2
Time to implement/ROI: Typically medium term and organisation-specific. An initial spend-based assessment can be undertaken relatively quickly using existing procurement data, while improving supplier-specific data and implementing procurement changes will generally take longer. ROI should compare the cost of measurement and supplier engagement with financial savings generated by resulting procurement changes; no universal payback period should be assumed.
Efficiency/Impact measure: Track % procurement spend mapped to emissions, % of priority suppliers providing primary emissions data, % of suppliers with emissions-reduction targets, and movement from spend-based estimates toward supplier-specific data. The GHG Protocol's Scope 3 guidance provides methods for progressively improving the quality of purchased-goods-and-services emissions calculations. Reference: https://ghgprotocol.org/scope-3-calculation-guidance-2
